L56: # Expo SDK reference
L57: 
L58: cite143†Edit page†github.com L59: 
L60: Copy page
L61: 
L62: Access device and system functionality in your Expo and React Native apps using Expo SDK packages.
L63: 
L64: * * *
L65: 
L66: The Expo SDK is a collection of packages that provide access to device and system functionality such as camera, contacts, location, sensors, haptics, and more. Each package targets a specific feature and can be used independently. All packages work in any React Native app with the `expo` package installed.
L67: You can install any Expo SDK package using the cite144†`npx expo install` command. For example, three different packages are installed using the following command:
L68: 
L69: Terminal
L70: 
L71: Copy
L72: 
L73: `- ``npx expo install expo-camera expo-contacts expo-sensors`
L74: 
L75: After installing one or more packages, you can import them into your JavaScript code:
L76: 
L77:     `import { CameraView } from 'expo-camera';
L78:     import { Contact } from 'expo-contacts';
L79:     import { Gyroscope } from 'expo-sensors';
L80:     `
L81: This allows you to write cite145†`Contact.getAll()` and read the contacts from the device, read the gyroscope sensor to detect device movement, or start the phone's camera and take photos.
L82: ## All Expo SDK packages work in any React Native app
L83: 
L84: Expo apps are React Native apps, so all Expo SDK packages work in any React Native app with the `expo` package installed and configured. The easiest way to create a React Native app with support for Expo SDK packages is to use `create-expo-app`. However, you can also add Expo SDK support to an existing React Native app with the `npx install-expo-modules` command.
L85: 
L86: Terminal
L87: 
L88: Copy
L89: 
L90: `# Create a project named my-app`
L91: `- ``npx create-expo-app my-app --template bare-minimum`
L92: 
L93: cite146†Install Expo SDK packages in existing React Native apps Learn more about configuring projects created with `npx @react-native-community/cli@latest init` to Expo SDK packages. cite147†Use libraries Learn how to install Expo SDK packages in your project. L94: ## Using pre-release versions
L95: 
L96: New Expo SDK versions are released three times each year. Between these releases, we publish pre-release versions of the `expo` package and all of the Expo SDK packages. Pre-releases are not considered stable and should only be used if you are comfortable with the risk of encountering bugs or other issues.
L97: ### Canary releases
L98: 
L99: Canary releases represent a snapshot of the state of the `main` branch at the time they are published. Canary package versions include `-canary` in the name, along with the date and commit hash, such as `57.0.0-canary-20260526-13e89ca`. To install the latest canary release:
L100: 
L101: Terminal
L102: 
L103: Copy
L104: 
L105: `# Install the alpha version of expo and its related packages`
L106: 
L107: `- ``npm install expo@canary && npx expo install --fix`
L108: You can often use pre-release versions of individual packages with stable releases of the Expo SDK. There may occasionally be incompatibilities or other issues that arise in canary-quality releases. You may want to cite148†silence dependency validation warnings if you opt in to the canary package and once you have verified that it works well for your use cases.
L109: ### Beta releases
L110: 
L111: Before each Expo SDK release, we publish beta versions of the `expo` package and all of the Expo SDK packages. Beta releases are considered much more stable than canary releases, and we encourage developers to try them out on their apps and share their feedback. Beta releases use the `beta` tag on npm and follow the instructions in the related cite2†changelog†expo.dev post.
L112: ## Each Expo SDK version depends on a React Native version
L113: 
L114: Expo SDK version  | React Native version  | React version  | React Native Web version  | React Native TV version  | Minimum Node.js version
L115: --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---
L116: 57.0.0  | 0.86  | 19.2.3  | 0.21.0  | 0.86-stable  | 22.13.x
L117: 56.0.0  | 0.85  | 19.2.3  | 0.21.0  | 0.85-stable  | 20.19.x
L118: 55.0.0  | 0.83  | 19.2.0  | 0.21.0  | 0.83-stable  | 20.19.x
L119: 54.0.0  | 0.81  | 19.1.0  | 0.21.0  | 0.81-stable  | 20.19.x
L120: ### Additional information
L121: 
L122: Expo SDK policy for tracking React Native releases
L123:   * Each Expo SDK release targets a single React Native version. This is typically the latest stable version at the time of the release.
L124:   * React Native currently has six releases per year and aims for every release to include no breaking changes.
L125:   * Expo SDK releases aim to follow this cadence.
L126:   * Pre-release versions of the upcoming Expo SDK will include support for the latest version of React Native quickly, usually the same day it is released. A member of the Expo SDK team works on the React Native releases team for each release, and is responsible for continuously updating the React Native version in the Expo repository, verifying compatibility, and reporting regressions back to the React Native team.
L127: What if I need a change from the latest React Native version and it's not yet in an Expo SDK release?
L128: 
L129: Expo engineers on the React Native releases team ensure that any urgent fixes are included in the React Native version used by the latest Expo SDK. If your specific fix won't be cherrypicked into an existing release, perhaps because it is not considered critical or because it involves a breaking change, then you have two options:
L130:   1. Use cite149†`patch-package`†github.com to pull in the fix.
L131:   2. Use a cite150†pre-release version of the Expo SDK .
L132: 
L133: Can I use an older version of React Native with the latest Expo SDK?
L134: Packages in the Expo SDK are intended to support the target React Native version for that SDK. Typically, they will not support older versions of React Native, but they may. When a new version of React Native is released, the latest versions of the Expo SDK packages are typically updated to support it. However, this may take weeks or more, depending on the extent of the changes in the release.
L135: ## Support for Android and iOS versions
L136: 
L137: Each version of Expo SDK supports a minimum OS version of Android and iOS. For Android, the `compileSdkVersion` is defined which tells the cite151†Gradle†developer.android.com which Android SDK version to use to compile the app. This also means that you can use the Android API features included in that SDK version and from the previous versions. For iOS, the cite152†Xcode†developer.apple.com tells the minimum Xcode SDK version to use to compile the app.
L138: Expo SDK version  | Android version  | `compileSdkVersion`  | `targetSdkVersion`  | iOS version  | Xcode version
L139: --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---
L140: 57.0.0  | 7+  | 36  | 36  | 16.4+  | 26.4+
L141: 56.0.0  | 7+  | 36  | 36  | 16.4+  | 26.4+
L142: 55.0.0  | 7+  | 36  | 36  | 15.1+  | 26.2+
L143: 54.0.0  | 7+  | 36  | 36  | 15.1+  | 16.1+
L144: When deciding whether to upgrade your Expo SDK version, consider both Expo's SDK version and app store submission requirements, as described in the above table. Google Play Store and Apple App Store periodically increase their minimum required OS versions and API levels, which are required for new app submissions. Expo has no control over the app store requirements, and you should check cite151†Google†developer.android.com and cite152†Apple†developer.apple.com for the current store submission requirements.
